{{Script/Arabic|اسم ڤدس}} | image = ASAM PEDAS IKAN PARI.jpg | image_size = 250px | caption = ''Asam pedas ikan pari'', a sour and spicy [[stingray]] stew | country = [[Maritime Southeast Asia]]{{Cite web|title=When the World Came to Southeast Asia: Malacca and the Global Economy|date=2014|url=https://www.asianstudies.org/publications/eaa/archives/when-the-world-came-to-southeast-asia-malacca-and-the-global-economy/|access-date=3 June 2025}}{{Cite book|last=Boi|first=Lee Geok|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OuBBDwAAQBAJ&q=asam+pedas+Indonesian+sour+and+spicy+dish&pg=PT49|title=Asian Seafood|date=15 September 2017|publisher=Marshall Cavendish International Asia Pte Ltd|isbn=978-981-4794-08-4|language=en}}{{Cite news|url= https://kebudayaan.kemdikbud.go.id/ditwdb/ikan-asam-pedas-pontianak-jenis-menu-masakan-masyarakat-melayu/|title=Ikan Asam Pedas Pontianak, Jenis menu masakan masyarakat Melayu|date=2 November 2020|website=idntimes.com|language=id|access-date=22 September 2020}}{{Cite news|url= https://kebudayaan.kemdikbud.go.id/bpnbkepri/pedasnya-ikan-asam-pedas-melayu/|title=Pedasnya Ikan Asam Pedas Melayu |last=Arman|first=Dedi|date=26 May 2019|website=kebudayaan.kemdikbud.go.id|language=id|access-date=22 September 2020}} | region = [[Sumatra]], [[Malay Peninsula]], [[Borneo]] | national_cuisine = [[Indonesian cuisine|Indonesia]], [[Malaysian cuisine|Malaysia]] and [[Singaporean cuisine|Singapore]] | creator = | course = Main course | served = Hot or room temperature | main_ingredient = Spicy, sour fish stew made with chillies and tamarind | variations = ''[[Gulai]]'', ''[[Kaeng som|Asam rebus]]'' | calories = | other = }} '''Asam pedas''' ([[Malay language|Malay]] for "sour spicy"; {{IPA|ms|ˌasam pəˈdas}}) is a traditional [[Taste|sour]] and [[Pungency|spicy]] ''[[gulai]]'' commonly found in [[Southeast Asia]], particularly in [[Malaysia]], [[Indonesia]] and [[Singapore]]. The dish is typically associated with [[Malay cuisine|Malay]], [[Padang cuisine|Minangkabau]], [[Acehnese cuisine|Acehnese]] and [[Peranakan cuisine]]s, and is prepared using various types of [[seafood]] or [[freshwater fish]]. The broth is made with a combination of [[Chili pepper|chillies]] and [[spice]]s, with the sour element derived from ingredients such as [[tamarind]], ''asam keping'' (dried ''[[Garcinia]]'' slices) or [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] juice, depending on regional variations. Regional names for the dish include ''asam padeh'' ([[Minangkabau language|Minangkabau]]), ''asam keueung'' ([[Acehnese language|Acehnese]]) and ''gerang asam'' ([[Malay trade and creole languages|Baba Malay]] or Peranakan). The development of ''asam pedas'' is commonly associated with several regions of [[maritime Southeast Asia]], notably the historic [[Entrepôt|trading port]] of [[Malacca City|Malacca]] in the [[Malay Peninsula]] and the [[Minangkabau people|Minangkabau heartlands]] of [[West Sumatra]]. These areas contributed to the evolution of the dish through long-standing [[Cultural diplomacy|cultural exchange]]s and [[Regional integration|regional trade network]]s. Influences from various culinary traditions led to the adaptation of local ingredients and cooking methods, resulting in distinct regional expressions of the dish. Today, ''asam pedas'' remains a widely prepared dish across [[Peninsular Malaysia]], [[Sumatra]], [[Borneo]] and the [[Riau Archipelago]]. The variations in ingredients, preparation techniques and flavour profiles across these areas reflect the diverse cultural and geographical contexts that have shaped its development.
